etymology: From Old English hālig (whole, sound, sacred), rendering Hebrew qādōsh (set apart, cut off) and Greek hagios; the holiness of God is His infinite separateness and moral purity.
biblical_def: The holiness of God is the crown and sum of His perfections—that attribute by which He is set infinitely apart from all that He has made, and infinitely pure in all that He is. When Isaiah was granted to see the LORD high and lifted up, the seraphim did not cry "eternal, eternal, eternal" nor "mighty, mighty, mighty," but "Holy, holy, holy"—the trisagion that ascribes to God a transcendent, threefold majesty before which the prophet was undone, crying, "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips." God's holiness is not merely one perfection among many; it is the very purity and exaltedness of His whole Being. It denotes His utter separation from creaturely limitation and His total separation from sin, for He is of purer eyes than to behold iniquity. To this holiness His people are summoned: "Be ye holy; for I am holy." The thrice-holy God dwells in light unapproachable, and yet, in sovereign grace, He sanctifies a people for Himself, conforming them to His own purity through the blood of Christ and the work of His Spirit. The 1689 Confession confesses Him "most holy in all His counsels, in all His works, and in all His commands." To know God truly is to tremble at His holiness and to flee to the Mediator who alone makes the unclean acceptable.
webster_summary: The state of being holy; purity or integrity of moral character; sanctity. Applied to God, it denotes His perfect and infinite purity and separateness from all evil.
webster_full: HOLINESS, n. From Old English hālig, whole, sound, sacred; the quality of being holy.
The state of being holy; purity or integrity of moral character; freedom from sin; sanctity.
Applied to the Supreme Being, holiness denotes perfect purity or integrity of the moral character; the absolute rectitude and infinite separateness of the divine nature.
The seraphim proclaim it of God alone: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory" (Isa 6:3).
Sacredness; the state of being hallowed or consecrated; that which is set apart unto God and His service.
scriptures: Isa 6:3
And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy.
Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.
Rev 4:8
And they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come.
corruption_summary: Modern sentimentality recasts God as indulgent affection, suppressing the holiness that makes His grace astonishing.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is not a single clever redefinition but a slow softening: God is reimagined as a benign well-wisher whose chief business is affirmation, until His holiness is felt as an embarrassment rather than His glory. A god who cannot be sinned against, who is never grieved, who makes no creature tremble, is an idol of human comfort. Such a god has no holiness to vindicate, and therefore no cross to require.

The principle to recover is that holiness is the atmosphere of heaven and the ground of all true worship. Isaiah's "Woe is me" is the only honest response to the thrice-holy God, and it is precisely the soul thus undone that hears, "thine iniquity is taken away." The 1689 Confession binds us to the God who is "most holy in all His counsels"; to behold that holiness is to flee to Christ, in whom alone the unclean are made to stand.
roots_summary: Holiness gathers the Hebrew idea of separateness and the moral idea of purity into one divine perfection.
roots_lines: Hebrew qādōsh — set apart, cut off, consecrated; the root of the trisagion.
Old English hālig — whole, sound, sacred; kin to "whole" and "hale."
Greek hagios — holy, separated unto God, the New Testament term for divine and saintly purity.
The trisagion ("Holy, holy, holy") is the only attribute Scripture lifts to the third degree.
Holiness joins the negative idea (separation from sin) to the positive (set apart unto God).
usage: Doctrinally, the holiness of God anchors the doctrine of sin, judgment, and the necessity of atonement.
Liturgically, the trisagion of Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4 frames all reverent, God-centered worship.
Pastorally, it teaches the believer to draw near with reverence and godly fear, never with presumption.

etymology: From Latin fidēs (faith, trust) through Old French feid, plus the native suffix; the faithfulness of God is His unfailing constancy to His own word and covenant.
biblical_def: The faithfulness of God is that perfection by which He is everlastingly true to Himself, to His word, and to His covenant, so that not one syllable of His promise can fall to the ground. Jeremiah, sitting amid the ashes of Jerusalem, finds the spring of hope precisely here: "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." God's faithfulness flows from His immutability; because He cannot change, He cannot break His word, and because He cannot lie, His covenant stands sure for a thousand generations. Paul anchors the believer's assurance in it: "God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son." Even our own faltering cannot overthrow it, for "if we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself." This faithfulness is not a bare reliability but a covenant loyalty—the steadfast love (Hebrew ḥesed) that keeps mercy for them that love Him. It is the bedrock of perseverance: He which hath begun a good work will perform it. The 1689 Confession rests every saving promise upon the God who is "abundant in goodness and truth." To trust the faithfulness of God is to lean the whole weight of the soul upon a Rock that has never once given way, and never can.
webster_summary: Firm adherence to truth and to duty; the quality of being true to one's word and engagements. Of God, His unfailing constancy in keeping His promises and covenant.
webster_full: FAITHFULNESS, n. From Latin fidēs, faith, trust; the quality of being faithful.
Fidelity; firm adherence to truth and to duty; the quality of keeping one's word, covenant, or engagement.
Truth; veracity; reliability; the disposition that may be entirely trusted and never deceives.
Of God, His unfailing constancy in performing His promises: "great is thy faithfulness" (Lam 3:23).
Loyal and steadfast love that abides though all else fail; covenant constancy.
scriptures: Lam 3:23
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.
If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.
Deu 7:9
Know therefore that the LORD thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations.
corruption_summary: No significant postmodern redefinition assails this attribute; the danger is rather practical unbelief that doubts God's word in the day of trouble.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The faithfulness of God is rarely attacked by argument; it is far more often eroded by the quiet unbelief of the heart, which in the day of darkness whispers that the promise has failed and the covenant is forgotten. Jeremiah himself wrote of God's faithfulness not from prosperity but from the smoking ruins of the city he loved.

The principle to recover is that God's faithfulness is grounded in His own unchanging nature, not in our circumstances or our feelings. Because He cannot deny Himself, His mercies are new every morning, and the saint may rest the whole weight of his perseverance upon a God who keeps covenant to a thousand generations. The 1689 Confession teaches that the work He begins He will surely perform—faithfulness is the cable that holds the anchor of hope.
roots_summary: Faithfulness joins the Hebrew idea of firmness with the covenant idea of loyal love.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ēmūnāh — firmness, steadiness, fidelity; the root behind "Amen."
Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast covenant love, often paired with faithfulness in the Psalms.
Latin fidēs — faith, trust, reliability; source of "faithful" and "fidelity."
Greek pistos — faithful, trustworthy; applied to God in 1 Corinthians 1:9.
"Amen" itself confesses the faithful God in whom every promise is yea and amen.
usage: Doctrinally, God's faithfulness grounds the certainty of His promises and the perseverance of the saints.
Pastorally, it is the believer's pillow in affliction—new mercies for every morning.
Liturgically, it is sung in confession and praise, as in the hymn "Great Is Thy Faithfulness."

etymology: From Latin favor (good will, kindness) through Old French favour; the favor of God is His gracious good pleasure resting upon His people in Christ.
biblical_def: The favor of God is His free, gracious good pleasure—the smile of His countenance resting upon those whom He loves in His Son. It is near kin to grace, for both name the unmerited kindness of God toward the undeserving, yet favor casts the warmth of a Father's pleasure over the relationship. The Psalmist sings, "For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield"—the favor of God is a defense that surrounds the whole man. Solomon declares that whoso findeth wisdom "shall obtain favour of the LORD," for to find true wisdom is to find Christ Himself, in whom the Father is well pleased. This favor is no reward earned by merit; it flows from the eternal good pleasure of God, who chose His people before the foundation of the world and accepted them in the Beloved. Even our Lord in His true humanity "increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man," that the Mediator might secure for His people the favor He alone perfectly deserved. To stand in the favor of God is to live under the lifted light of His countenance, justified, adopted, and kept. The 1689 Confession traces every spiritual benefit to this fountain of free, unchanging divine good pleasure. The believer's confidence is not that he has earned a smile, but that the smile rests upon Christ, and upon him in Christ.
webster_summary: Kind regard; good will; the disposition to oblige or benefit. Of God, His gracious good pleasure and acceptance bestowed freely upon His people.
webster_full: FAVOR, n. From Latin favor, good will, kindness; kind regard or benevolent disposition.
Kind regard; good will; countenance; the disposition to befriend, oblige, or benefit another.
Acceptance; the state of being approved and well-pleasing; the lifting up of one's countenance upon another.
Of God, His gracious good pleasure freely bestowed: "with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield" (Ps 5:12).
A gift, kindness, or benefit conferred out of good will rather than owed as a debt.
scriptures: Psa 5:12
For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield.
Pro 8:35
For whoso findeth me findeth life, and shall obtain favour of the LORD.
Luk 2:52
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
Psa 30:5
For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
corruption_summary: No genuine postmodern redefinition besets this term; the recurring error is treating divine favor as wages for performance rather than free grace in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The favor of God is not so much twisted by ideology as cheapened by a works-righteousness that imagines God's smile must be purchased by sufficient effort, or by a presumption that takes His kindness for granted. Both forget that favor, like grace, is free and rests upon the merit of Another.

The principle to recover is that the favor of God flows from His eternal good pleasure and is secured for His people by Christ, who alone perfectly increased in favor with God. The believer is "accepted in the beloved," compassed about with favor as with a shield. The 1689 Confession grounds every blessing in this free and unchanging good pleasure—to walk in God's favor is to walk in the lifted light of His countenance, given, not earned.
roots_summary: Favor blends the Latin idea of benevolent good will with the biblical idea of free grace.
roots_lines: Latin favor — good will, kindness, support; source of "favorable" and "favorite."
Hebrew rāṣōn — good pleasure, acceptance, delight; the LORD's favorable regard.
Hebrew ḥēn — grace, favor, charm; the unmerited kindness shown to the lowly.
Greek charis — grace, favor; the New Testament word uniting favor and grace.
"Favour" in the KJV often translates the same words rendered elsewhere as "grace."
usage: Doctrinally, the favor of God is closely allied to grace and to the doctrine of free acceptance in Christ.
Pastorally, it assures the saint that God's countenance is lifted upon him for Christ's sake.
Devotionally, it answers the Aaronic blessing—"the LORD lift up his countenance upon thee."

etymology: From Latin pater (father) and misericordia (mercy, compassion); the title renders Paul's Greek patēr tōn oiktirmōn, naming God as the source and fountain of all compassion.
biblical_def: "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort." This is Paul's great doxology, and in it he names God by a title that opens the very fountainhead of compassion. To call God the Father of mercies is to say that He is the source, the parent, the begetter of every mercy that has ever fallen upon a sinful world—not one mercy comes but from His hand, and He is rich in mercy without measure. The plural, "mercies," gathers up the manifold and tender compassions of God, His oiktirmoi, the yearning of the bowels of divine pity toward the afflicted. He is likewise "the God of all comfort," who comforts us in all our tribulation that we may be able to comfort others. This title shines brightest against the backdrop of judgment, for the same God who is most holy is also most merciful, and these perfections meet without contradiction in the cross of Christ, where mercy and truth embrace. The mercies of the Father are no fickle moods but the steady overflow of His covenant love, ever near to the broken-hearted. The 1689 Confession confesses Him "most loving, gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness." To the trembling and the comfortless, this name is a refuge: the throne of grace is the seat of the Father of mercies, and they that come find compassion that never runs dry.
webster_summary: A title of God expressing that He is the source and fountain of all compassion and tender pity; the God of all comfort.
webster_full: FATHER OF MERCIES, title. From Latin pater, father, and misericordia, mercy; the scriptural name of God as the source of all compassion.
A title ascribing to God the origin and abundance of all mercy, as a father is the source of his offspring.
Expressing the tender, manifold compassions of God toward the afflicted and the penitent.
Paul's doxology: "the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort" (2Co 1:3).
Denoting that mercy flows from God not by chance but by His very nature and fatherly disposition.
scriptures: Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort.
Eph 2:4
But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us.
Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him.
Lam 3:22
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition assails this title; the danger is severing mercy from holiness, as though God's pity required no atoning satisfaction.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chief error touching the Father of mercies is not ideological but theological: to imagine a mercy that simply overlooks sin, a fatherly pity that needs no cross. Such sentimental mercy makes light of the holiness it must honor and empties the death of Christ of its necessity.

The principle to recover is that the mercy of the Father flows to sinners through the satisfaction of the Son, where mercy and truth meet together. The God who is "rich in mercy" is rich precisely because that mercy cost the blood of His own Son. The 1689 Confession confesses Him "most merciful" alongside "most holy and just"—the Father of mercies is no indulgent sentiment but the covenant compassion that pardons the guilty in Christ.
roots_summary: The title joins fatherhood and compassion to name God as the wellspring of all mercy.
roots_lines: Greek patēr — father; here the source or originator, as "father of lights."
Greek oiktirmos — compassion, tender pity; the plural "mercies" of 2 Corinthians 1:3.
Hebrew raḥamīm — tender mercies, from the word for the womb; deep yearning pity.
Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast covenant love, often joined with mercy and compassion.
The plural "mercies" signals the manifold and inexhaustible compassions of God.
usage: Doctrinally, the title grounds the doctrine of God's mercy and the comfort of the afflicted saint.
Pastorally, it directs the broken-hearted to a God whose compassions fail not.
Liturgically, it opens many prayers and blessings as the address of the comfortless to their God.

etymology: From Latin in- (not) and comparabilis (able to be compared); the incomparable God is He to whom nothing in heaven or earth may be likened.
biblical_def: The incomparable God is the LORD who stands alone, to whom no creature, no idol, and no rival may be compared. "To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?" cries Isaiah, and again, "To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One." The question admits no answer, for God is in a class wholly His own—underived, self-existent, infinite, eternal. Moses and Israel sang it at the Red Sea: "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?" This incomparability is the root of the first commandment and the death-blow to all idolatry, for every false god is a creature of the imagination, while the LORD alone is God and beside Him there is none else. His transcendence means He is not the highest member of a class but the only Being of His kind; He dwells in unapproachable light, measuring the waters in the hollow of His hand and meting out heaven with the span. Yet this incomparable God stoops in mercy, condescending to dwell with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit. The 1689 Confession confesses one only living and true God, infinite in being and perfection, a most pure Spirit, invisible, immutable, immense. To worship the incomparable God is to give Him the glory due unto His name, and to bow before a majesty that has no equal and can have none.
webster_summary: That cannot be compared; matchless; having no equal. Of God, the perfection by which He transcends and is unlike all created things.
webster_full: INCOMPARABLE, adj. From Latin in-, not, and comparabilis, that may be compared; matchless.
That admits of no comparison with others; matchless; peerless; having no equal.
Of supreme excellence; so far surpassing all else that no parallel can be drawn.
Of God, the perfection by which He is unlike all creatures: "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?" (Exo 15:11).
Transcendent; beyond measure or rival; standing alone in a class peculiar to itself.
scriptures: To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?
To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One.
Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?
Isa 46:9
Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition besets this truth directly; the perennial assault is idolatry, which dethrones the incomparable God by likening Him to the creature.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The incomparability of God is not refuted by argument so much as denied in practice by every idolatry, ancient and modern, that fashions a god in the image of the creature—whether of wood and stone, or of sentiment and imagination. To liken God to anything made is to commit the very sin Isaiah's questions expose.

The principle to recover is the sheer transcendence and aseity of God: He is not the greatest of beings but the only Being of His kind, self-existent and beside whom there is none else. The 1689 Confession confesses Him infinite in being and perfection, a most pure Spirit. To know Him truly is to abandon every likeness and to bow before a majesty that has no equal and can have none.
roots_summary: The phrase names the truth that God transcends all comparison and stands alone as God.
roots_lines: Latin comparabilis — able to be matched or paired; negated by in-.
Hebrew mī-kāmōkā — "who is like thee," the song of Moses at the sea.
Hebrew 'ēn kāmōkā — "there is none like thee," a refrain of incomparability.
Greek monos theos — the only God; the New Testament confession of His uniqueness.
Incomparability undergirds the first commandment and the rejection of all idols.
usage: Doctrinally, the incomparable God grounds divine transcendence, aseity, and the rejection of idolatry.
Liturgically, it is sung in the Song of the Sea and echoed in Israel's confessions of the one true God.
Apologetically, it answers every attempt to liken God to the creature or to a rival deity.

etymology: From Latin inspirare (to breathe into), rendering Paul's Greek theopneustos (God-breathed); inspiration is the act by which God breathed out His Word through chosen men.
biblical_def: The inspiration of Scripture is that supernatural work whereby God so superintended the human authors of the Bible that, using their own minds, styles, and circumstances, they wrote without error the very words God intended—so that the product is in truth the Word of God. Paul states it directly: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God," literally God-breathed, theopneustos, exhaled from the mouth of God Himself. Peter unfolds the manner: "the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost," borne along as a ship is carried by the wind. This is verbal plenary inspiration: verbal, because it extends to the very words and not merely the thoughts; plenary, because it reaches every part, from Genesis to Revelation, equally and fully. Such inspiration secures inerrancy—the Scriptures, in their original autographs, are without error in all they affirm—and undergirds sola scriptura, that the Bible alone is the supreme and sufficient rule of faith and life. The men were not passive pens, yet neither were they free authors; the Spirit moved them so that what they wrote, God said. The 1689 Confession confesses the Holy Scripture to be "given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life." To receive the Bible as God-breathed is to bow to its every word as to the voice of the living God, who cannot lie and does not err.
webster_summary: The supernatural influence of the Spirit of God upon the writers of Scripture, by which they were qualified to communicate divine truth without error; the quality of being God-breathed.
webster_full: INSPIRATION, n. From Latin inspirare, to breathe into; the act of breathing in.
The infusion of ideas or supernatural influence into the mind by the Spirit of God.
The communication of divine truth to the sacred writers, such that what they wrote is the very word of God.
Paul's testimony: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine" (2Ti 3:16).
The God-breathed quality of Holy Scripture, extending to its very words and to all its parts.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken.
corruption_summary: The historical-critical method denies that Scripture is God-breathed, reducing it to a merely human record of evolving religion and dissolving its inerrant authority.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the historical-critical denial of inspiration, which treats the Bible as a purely human collection of religious literature—layered, edited, and contradictory—rather than the God-breathed Word. On this view, "inspiration" means at most that the writers were religiously gifted men, and the text records their evolving ideas about God rather than God's own self-revelation. Stripped of its divine authorship, Scripture becomes an artifact to be dissected rather than a voice to be obeyed, and the believer is left to sift the "authentic" from the "legendary" by the shifting standards of the critic.

The principle to recover is verbal plenary inspiration: Scripture is theopneustos, breathed out by God through holy men borne along by the Holy Ghost, true and without error in all it affirms. Because God is its ultimate Author, the Scripture cannot be broken. The 1689 Confession grounds the whole authority of the Bible "wholly upon God, the author thereof"—to deny inspiration is to silence the voice of God and enthrone the autonomous critic in His place. Sola scriptura stands or falls here.
roots_summary: Inspiration centers on the God-breathed character of the written Word.
roots_lines: Greek theopneustos — God-breathed; the one word behind 2 Timothy 3:16.
Greek pherō (as pheromenoi) — borne along, carried, as a ship by the wind (2 Pet 1:21).
Latin inspirare — to breathe into; source of the English "inspiration."
Verbal plenary inspiration — extending to the very words (verbal) and to every part (plenary).
Inspiration secures inerrancy and undergirds the doctrine of sola scriptura.
usage: Doctrinally, inspiration is the foundation of biblical authority, inerrancy, and sufficiency.
Apologetically, it answers the historical-critical reduction of Scripture to mere human literature.
Pastorally, it teaches the saint to receive every word of the Bible as the voice of God.

etymology: From Old English hālig (holy) and Latin scriptura (a writing); the Holy Scriptures are the sacred writings of the Old and New Testaments, set apart as the Word of God.
biblical_def: The Holy Scriptures are the sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments, given by the inspiration of God, and constituting the whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life. Paul reminds Timothy "that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus." They are called holy because they are set apart from all other writings, breathed out by the holy God, and consecrated to a holy end—the salvation and sanctification of sinners. The canon is closed and complete: the thirty-nine books of the Old Testament and the twenty-seven of the New, no more and no less, recognized by the church as the very oracles of God. As the supreme rule of faith and practice, the Scriptures stand above pope, council, and tradition—sola scriptura—for they alone carry the authority of their divine Author. They are sufficient, needing no addition; perspicuous in all things necessary to salvation, so that the unlearned may understand; and efficacious, the very instrument by which the Spirit makes wise unto salvation. The 1689 Confession opens by confessing "the Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience." To hold the Holy Scriptures is to hold in one's hand the living and abiding Word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.
webster_summary: The sacred writings of the Old and New Testaments; the inspired and authoritative books constituting the Word of God and the rule of faith and life.
webster_full: SCRIPTURE, n. From Latin scriptura, a writing; with "holy," the sacred writings.
Appropriately and by way of distinction, the books of the Old and New Testaments; the Bible.
The inspired Word of God, set apart as holy and constituting the supreme rule of faith and obedience.
Paul's charge: "the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation" (2Ti 3:15).
The whole canon of sixty-six books recognized by the church as the oracles of God.
scriptures: And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Rom 1:2
Which he had promised afore by his prophets in the holy scriptures.
Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
But the word of the Lord endureth for ever. And this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you.
corruption_summary: Modern movements set tradition, experience, or the autonomous self alongside or above Scripture, overthrowing its unique and sufficient authority.
corruption_paragraphs: The persistent corruption is the denial of sola scriptura: the elevation of church tradition, ecclesiastical office, private experience, or the reader's own intuitions to a place beside or above the written Word. Wherever an authority is set up that may correct, supplement, or silence the Scriptures, their unique supremacy is overthrown, and the conscience is delivered back into bondage to the doctrines and commandments of men.

The principle to recover is that the Holy Scriptures alone are the sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience. They are able to make wise unto salvation, they are profitable for doctrine and correction, and the word of the Lord endureth for ever. The 1689 Confession rests the whole of the Christian religion upon this single foundation—the canon is closed, the Word is sufficient, and to it nothing is to be added at any time, whether by new revelations or the traditions of men.
roots_summary: The phrase joins holiness with the written Word to name the consecrated books of God.
roots_lines: Greek graphē — a writing, Scripture; the New Testament term for the sacred text.
Greek hiera grammata — "holy scriptures," the very phrase of 2 Timothy 3:15.
Latin scriptura — a writing; source of the English "Scripture."
Old English hālig — holy, set apart; marking the writings as consecrated to God.
"Canon" (Greek kanōn, a rule) names the closed list of sixty-six inspired books.
usage: Doctrinally, the Holy Scriptures are the formal principle of the Reformation—sola scriptura.
Practically, they are the saint's daily lamp, sufficient for faith and obedience.
Confessionally, they open the 1689 Confession as the only infallible rule of saving knowledge.

etymology: From the Epistle of Paul to the Galatians, chapter three, verse twenty-eight; a charter text of justifying union with Christ across every human distinction.
biblical_def: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." This is one of the great charter texts of the gospel, and its true sense is gloriously clear from its context. Paul has been arguing that justification is by faith and not by works of the law; here he declares that all who are baptized into Christ have "put on Christ," so that with respect to justification, adoption, and inheritance, no creaturely distinction confers advantage or disadvantage. Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female stand on the identical footing before God: all are justified by the same faith, washed by the same blood, indwelt by the same Spirit, and made "heirs according to the promise." The verse speaks to standing in Christ, not to the abolition of God's good creational order. It does not erase the distinction between Jew and Gentile in redemptive history, nor between master and servant in the household, nor between male and female in marriage, family, and church—for the same apostle who wrote this verse also taught male headship in the home and reserved the office of elder to qualified men. Equal standing in justification and unequal callings in the created order are no contradiction; they meet in the same harmonious wisdom of God. The 1689 Confession upholds both: one salvation freely given to all who believe, and an ordered church and household governed by the Word.
webster_summary: A verse of Paul's Epistle to the Galatians declaring that all believers, regardless of nation, station, or sex, share one and the same standing in justification and inheritance in Christ.
webster_full: GALATIANS 3:28, scripture reference. From Paul's Epistle to the Galatians; a charter text of union with Christ.
A declaration that in the matter of justification and inheritance, no distinction of nation, rank, or sex confers advantage before God.
Set in Paul's argument that righteousness is by faith and not by works of the law.
The verse itself: "there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28).
Affirming equal standing in salvation while leaving intact the created order of callings.
scriptures: Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Gal 3:26
For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus.
Gal 3:29
And if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise.
But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
corruption_summary: The egalitarian movement misuses this verse to abolish the creational order of male headship and male-only eldership, reading a statement about justifying standing as a leveling of office and calling.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the egalitarian misreading that wrenches "neither male nor female" out of its context to overturn the order God wove into creation. On this view, equal standing in Christ is made to mean the erasure of all distinction in calling, so that male headship in marriage and the reservation of the eldership to qualified men are dismissed as relics of bygone culture. But this reads into a sentence about justification a doctrine of office it was never given to teach, and it pits Paul against himself—for the same apostle, by the same Spirit, forbade a woman to teach or usurp authority over the man.

The principle to recover is that equal standing in justification does not abolish the creational order of headship. Jew and Greek are one in Christ, yet redemptive history retains its order; slave and free are one, yet the household keeps its callings; male and female are equally heirs of grace, yet God assigns distinct and complementary roles in marriage and church. The 1689 Confession holds both without strain: one salvation for all who believe, and an ordered church governed by qualified men. To flatten the verse into a charter for overturning that order is to honor neither the text nor its Author.
roots_summary: The verse turns on union with Christ as the ground of equal standing among diverse believers.
roots_lines: Greek heis — one; "ye are all one" (heis) in Christ Jesus.
Greek en Christōi — "in Christ," the sphere of union and justifying standing.
Greek enedusasthe — "ye have put on" Christ, as a garment (Gal 3:27).
The threefold pairing (Jew/Greek, bond/free, male/female) spans nation, station, and sex.
Context is justification by faith—standing before God, not the ordering of callings.
usage: Doctrinally, the verse teaches equal standing in justification and inheritance for all believers.
Confessionally, it harmonizes with male headship and male-only eldership taught elsewhere by Paul.
Apologetically, it answers the egalitarian misuse that would abolish the created order.

etymology: From Latin precari (to beg, entreat) and Old English fæstan (to abstain from food); the joining of earnest prayer with abstinence in seasons of seeking God.
biblical_def: Prayer and fasting is the joining of earnest, importunate prayer with the voluntary abstinence from food, that the soul may humble itself and give itself wholly to the seeking of God. Our Lord taught that certain spiritual battles yield to no lesser exercise: "Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting." Fasting is no meritorious work, and it does not bend the will of God by its own power; rather, it is the body's servant to the soul's earnestness, a setting aside of lawful comforts that the whole man may bend himself to prayer with undivided attention and self-denying gravity. The early church practiced it at every solemn juncture. When the Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work, "they had fasted and prayed" and laid their hands on them; and as they ordained elders in every church, "they prayed with fasting, and commended them to the Lord." Thus fasting accompanies the great decisions of the church—the sending of missionaries, the setting apart of officers, seasons of repentance and of seeking guidance. It is to be done not for the eyes of men but unto the Father, in lowliness and sincerity. The 1689 Confession numbers "solemn humiliations, with fastings" among the parts of religious worship to be used in a holy and religious manner. Prayer and fasting, then, is the posture of a church and a soul that means business with God—hungering after Him more than after bread.
webster_summary: The religious exercise of joining earnest prayer with abstinence from food, practiced in seasons of solemn seeking, repentance, or important decision.
webster_full: FASTING, n. From Old English fæstan, to abstain; voluntary abstinence from food joined with prayer.
The act of abstaining from food, especially as a religious duty united with prayer and humiliation.
A solemn exercise of devotion in which the body is denied that the soul may seek God the more earnestly.
Practiced by the church at solemn junctures: "they prayed with fasting, and commended them to the Lord" (Act 14:23).
Not a meritorious work, but a help to fervent prayer and an expression of humble dependence.
scriptures: Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.
Act 13:3
And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Joe 2:12
Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition assails this discipline; the abiding dangers are neglect on the one hand and a merit-seeking, outward formalism on the other.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruptions of prayer and fasting are old, not new. On one side lies simple neglect, as though the discipline belonged to a former age and had no place in the believer's life today. On the other lies the hypocrite's fast that Isaiah and our Lord both rebuked—an outward show of abstinence, paraded before men, divorced from a humbled heart and earnest prayer.

The principle to recover is that fasting is the servant of prayer, not a meritorious work—a setting aside of lawful comforts so that the whole man may seek God with undivided earnestness. Practiced unto the Father in secret, joined to importunate prayer at solemn junctures, it humbles the soul and presses it upon God. The 1689 Confession numbers solemn humiliations with fastings among the duties of worship; the church does well to keep them in seasons of repentance, decision, and the setting apart of her officers.
roots_summary: The phrase pairs the act of entreaty with the act of abstinence in the service of seeking God.
roots_lines: Greek nēsteia — fasting, abstinence from food; the term in Acts and the Gospels.
Greek proseuchē — prayer; joined with fasting in Matthew 17:21.
Old English fæstan — to abstain, hold fast; source of the English "fast."
Hebrew ṣōm — to fast, to abstain from food in mourning or supplication.
Fasting accompanies the church's solemn acts: missions, ordination, repentance, and seeking guidance.
usage: Doctrinally, prayer and fasting belongs to the means and parts of religious worship.
Ecclesially, it attends the sending of missionaries and the ordination of elders.
Devotionally, it humbles the soul in seasons of repentance and earnest seeking of God.

etymology: From Latin privatus (set apart, one's own) and precari (to entreat); private prayer is the secret converse of the soul with God, apart from the eyes of men.
biblical_def: Private prayer is the secret converse of the believing soul with God, offered apart from the eyes of men, in the closet of the heart and the chamber of the house. Our Lord taught it plainly: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly." Here is the very heart of the devotional life—not the prayer that performs for an audience, but the prayer that seeks the face of the Father alone. The closet door, shut against the world, shuts out also the hypocrite's temptation to be seen of men, that the soul may deal with God in simplicity and truth. Such prayer is the breath of the regenerate, the appointed means by which the saint casts every care upon God, confesses sin, pleads the promises, and holds communion with his heavenly Father through the one Mediator. Our Lord Himself, who needed no rebuke of hypocrisy, withdrew to solitary places and continued all night in prayer to God, leaving His people a pattern of secret devotion. The Father "which seeth in secret" observes the hidden groanings and the unspoken desires, and answers openly in His own time and way. The 1689 Confession names prayer, made "in the name of the Son, by the help of the Spirit, according to His will," as a part of natural worship due to God. Private prayer is the secret root from which all public godliness must grow.
webster_summary: Secret prayer offered to God in solitude, apart from the observation of men; the personal and devotional communion of the soul with its heavenly Father.
webster_full: PRAYER, n. From Latin precari, to entreat; with "private," secret devotion offered alone.
The act of addressing God in supplication, confession, and communion, performed in solitude and secrecy.
The personal and devotional intercourse of the believing soul with God, hidden from the eyes of men.
Our Lord's charge: "enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret" (Mat 6:6).
The secret root of godliness, observed and rewarded by the Father who seeth in secret.
scriptures: Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Luk 6:12
And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.
Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
Phi 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition besets private prayer; its perennial enemies are the hypocrisy that prays to be seen and the busyness that crowds out the secret closet.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Private prayer is not the target of ideological revision; it is rather quietly abandoned. Its ancient enemy is the hypocrisy our Lord exposed—the prayer performed for the admiration of men—and its modern enemy is the crowded, distracted life that leaves no room for the shut door and the seeking of God in secret.

The principle to recover is that the closet, shut against the world, is the cradle of all true godliness. The Father who seeth in secret is the One the believer is to seek, casting every care upon Him through the one Mediator, by the help of the Spirit. The 1689 Confession names prayer a part of the worship due to God; our Lord's own withdrawal to solitary places is the saint's pattern. Public devotion can only be as deep as the secret prayer that feeds it.
roots_summary: The phrase joins secrecy with prayer to name the hidden communion of the soul with God.
roots_lines: Greek tameion — inner chamber, storeroom, "closet"; the secret place of Matthew 6:6.
Greek proseuchomai — to pray; the verb of addressing God in worship.
Latin privatus — one's own, set apart; source of the English "private."
Latin precari — to entreat, beg; source of "prayer" and "precarious."
"The Father which seeth in secret" is the One to whom private prayer is addressed.
usage: Doctrinally, private prayer is a part of the natural worship due to God from every creature.
Devotionally, it is the secret root and daily breath of the believer's communion with God.
Pastorally, it guards against hypocrisy by seeking the Father's face rather than the praise of men.
